articles.title: Firecrackers still Delhi’s top pollutant after Deepavali, IITM finds
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: The contribution of firecrackers to the city's pollution levels was significantly higher on November 9, a day after Deepavali, before declining on November 11, the IITM models showed

Firecrackers emerged as the biggest contributor to Delhi's air pollution on both Monday (November 9, 2026) and Tuesday (November 10), accounting for 71.1% and 29.8% of the pollution load, respectively, according to source-apportionment estimates by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM).

The contribution of firecrackers to the city's pollution levels was significantly higher on Monday (November 9), a day after Deepavali, before declining on Tuesday (November 11), the IITM models showed.

The estimates had a standard deviation (SD) of 104.1 percentage points on Monday (November 9) and 27.7 percentage points on Tuesday (November 10), indicating considerable variability and uncertainty in the modelled contributions.

On Monday (November 9), vehicular emissions accounted for 6.9% of the pollution, followed by secondary inorganic aerosols at 5% and secondary organic aerosols at 4.5%. Mixed or unresolved biofuel contributed 4.45%, while mineral dust and ash and mixed combustion accounted for 2.5% each.

Wood burning contributed 1.3%, while waste burning, including municipal and plastic-rubber-containing waste, accounted for 1.1%. Coal combustion and industrial emissions contributed 0.5% and 0.2%, respectively.
On Tuesday (November 10), the contribution of firecrackers dropped to 29.8%, while secondary organic aerosols emerged as the second-largest contributor at 17.5%.
Vehicular emissions and secondary inorganic aerosols each accounted for 11.7% of the pollution load, while wood burning contributed 10.7% and waste burning 7.7%.
Vehicular emissions emerged as the third largest contributor to pollution on Tuesday (November 10).
Mixed combustion accounted for 5.1%, followed by mixed or unresolved biofuel at 3.3% and mineral dust and ash at 1.5%.
Delhi's average 24-hour Air Quality Index (AQI) had improved marginally to the 'poor' category on Tuesday (November 10), with the 4 p.m. reading settling at 299.

Wood burning contributed 1.3%, while waste burning, including municipal and plastic-rubber-containing waste, accounted for 1.1%. Coal combustion and industrial emissions contributed 0.5% and 0.2%, respectively.

On Tuesday (November 10), the contribution of firecrackers dropped to 29.8%, while secondary organic aerosols emerged as the second-largest contributor at 17.5%.

Vehicular emissions and secondary inorganic aerosols each accounted for 11.7% of the pollution load, while wood burning contributed 10.7% and waste burning 7.7%.

Vehicular emissions emerged as the third largest contributor to pollution on Tuesday (November 10).

Mixed combustion accounted for 5.1%, followed by mixed or unresolved biofuel at 3.3% and mineral dust and ash at 1.5%.

Delhi's average 24-hour Air Quality Index (AQI) had improved marginally to the 'poor' category on Tuesday (November 10), with the 4 p.m. reading settling at 299.

articles.title: WhatsApp to simplify communication on app, add financial services
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Meta’s head of WhatsApp Kunal Shah shared a post outlining some largely expected outcomes for the messaging platform
Meta’s new head of WhatsApp, Kunal Shah, has promised simplified calls/messages and more financial services on the messaging platform, apart from increased AI integration.
In a post on the social media platform X on Tuesday (November 10, 2026), Mr. Shah said he had spent around four months at WhatsApp.
He also shared some largely expected goals for the platform.
The WhatsApp executive said he would make voice notes, groups, stickers and video “simpler and more expressive.”

The company is also working with financial services and telecom partners to explore processes such as paying bills, borrowing money, and ensuring connectivity during travel. The aim of this step is to keep users within the messaging platform, even if they are completing other personal finance tasks.
Not surprisingly, Mr. Shah said he wanted to make these features more efficient with AI.
He did not announce any specific features or share a release date for the same.
WhatsApp handles over 100 billion messages and 2 billion calls every day, he shared, while stressing that the company’s principles would not change any time soon.

“Your personal messages and calls stay end-to-end encrypted. This and our quality bar stays the same. What happens inside WhatsApp only matters for what it makes possible outside it: more time together, stronger communities, and fewer barriers between people and the lives they want to live,” shared Mr. Shah.

articles.title: Faith meets fitness: The Keralam church where prayers come with pull-ups
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, has set up an open gym to promote fitness among parishioners. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass

At St. Joseph’s Church in Kuriachira, Thrissur, Keralam, faith and fitness go hand in hand. An open gym on the church premises is drawing parishioners of all ages to stretch, sweat and stay fit. The unusual initiative is adding a healthy new dimension to church life.

Set up in a corner of the church campus, the facility has quickly become a meeting point for fitness enthusiasts. With no fixed timings, parishioners can drop in at their convenience, with many heading to the gym after attending Holy Mass. The altar boys, numbering around 60, are among its regular users. Parents also bring their young children, while senior citizens use the basic equipment to stay active.

The initiative has its roots in the personal fitness routine of the church’s vicar, Fr. Frederick Eluvathingal, 69. A footballer and basketball player during his student days, he has never allowed age or a demanding schedule to come in the way of exercise.

“I have been working out for the past 51 years, ever since my days at the Papal Seminary in Pune,” he says. His fitness routine continued during his higher studies in Rome and Jerusalem and his church assignments in Australia.

When he arrived at Kuriachira more than a year ago, he began looking for a suitable space to continue his regular exercises, including push-ups and pull-ups. Parallel bars were installed first, followed by a basketball hoop. The idea gradually grew into a community gym.

“I wanted to create a space where people could develop the habit of working out. We generally do not have a strong workout culture. If people can fit in some basic exercise when they come to church, they may gradually make fitness part of their lives,” he says.

The need is particularly pressing at a time when lifestyle diseases and obesity are on the rise. The initiative also seeks to draw more youngsters into church activities and channel their energy into constructive pursuits.

The parish welcomed the proposal, and a space around a well on the church premises was chosen for the facility. The limited space available in Kuriachira meant that the gym had to be modest, but the response has been encouraging.
“Within a week of starting the gym, quite a few people began coming here. If the demand grows, we will have to think about expanding the facility,” says P.R. Wilson, one of the church trustees.

For regular user John Vazhappilly, a real estate broker who lives nearby, the gym has come as a timely help. “I have been coming here every evening for the past week. After an accident and surgery, the muscles in my leg became weak. I want to strengthen them. This is a comfortable place to exercise, with fresh air and an open campus,” he says.

articles.title: Kedarnath temple portals closed for winter; deity's palanquin begins journey to Ukhimath
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The process began at 4 a.m. with special prayers and religious ceremonies, with all rituals performed in accordance with traditional customs before the temple doors were closed at the auspicious time
The portals of the Kedarnath shrine were closed for the winter season at 8.30 a.m. on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) following prescribed rituals and the chanting of Vedic mantras.

The process began at 4 a.m. with special prayers and religious ceremonies, with all rituals performed in accordance with traditional customs before the temple doors were closed at the auspicious time.
Following the closure, the processional palanquin of Lord Kedarnath was carried around the temple complex before departing for the Omkareshwar Temple in Ukhimath, the deity's winter abode.

According to the schedule, the palanquin will halt overnight at Rampur on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) before reaching Guptkashi on November 12. It will arrive at the Omkareshwar Temple in Ukhimath on November 13.
For the next six months, devotees can offer prayers to the deity at the Omkareshwar Temple.
The ceremonial palanquin of Goddess Yamuna, led by Shani Dev Maharaj, departed from Yamunotri for Kharsali, the deity’s winter abode, amid traditional rituals and folk music.
Villagers and pilgrims accorded a grand welcome to the palanquin upon its arrival in the afternoon at the ancestral village of the goddess, showering it with flowers and garlands.
During the six-month pilgrimage season, the Yamunotri Temple Committee received more than ₹90 lakh in donations through donation boxes and receipt books.

On Tuesday (November 10, 2026), a day before the closure of the temple, the committee opened the donation boxes for the fourth time to count the offerings. The exercise yielded ₹10 lakh 42 thousand in cash, while approximately ₹6 lakh was collected through receipt books.

articles.title: Jagan alleges large-scale malpractice in Andhra local body polls; says YSRCP vote share rose
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: YSRCP leaders allege bouncers at counting centres, rejected votes and recounts that changed results

YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) president and former Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy has accused the Telugu Desam Party (TDP-led) government of resorting to large-scale electoral malpractice in the recent local body elections to conceal the growing public support for his party.

At a meeting with party leaders from several districts at Tadepalli on Wednesday (November 11, 2026), Mr. Jagan reviewed the conduct of the elections and alleged that irregularities, intimidation and manipulation had taken place at various stages of the electoral process, from the announcement of the schedule to the counting of votes.

మున్సిపల్, ఎంపీటీసీ, జెడ్పీటీసీ ఎన్నికలు జరిగిన తీరుపై పార్టీ కేంద్ర కార్యాలయంలో వివిధ జిల్లా నాయకులతో కలిసి సమీక్షించిన వైయస్ జగన్ గారు టీడీపీ దౌర్జన్యాలు, దాడులకి ఎదురు నిలిచి నాయకులతో పాటు కార్యకర్తలు గట్టిగా పోరాటం చేశారని వైయస్ జగన్ గారు కితాబు ఎన్నికలు సజావుగా జరిగి ఉంటే వైయస్‌‌ఆర్‌సీపీ ఓటింగ్ శాతం ఇంకా పెరిగేదన్న వైయస్ జగన్ గారు.. చంద్రబాబు ప్రభుత్వం తప్పుల్ని కప్పిపుచ్చుకోవడానికి అక్రమాలకి పాల్పడిందని మండిపాటు తమ రాజకీయ జీవితంలో ఈ తరహాలో ఎన్నికల్లో అక్రమాలను చూడలేదని వైయస్ జగన్ గారికి చెప్పిన పార్టీ సీనియర్ నేతలు

The YSRCP’s vote share had increased compared with the 2024 elections despite the alleged irregularities, he said. The party would have secured a much higher vote share had the elections been conducted in a free and fair manner, he added.

Accusing Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu of misusing official machinery, Mr. Jagan said the ruling party had resorted to undemocratic practices because of the growing support for the YSRCP and the declining popularity of the government. New methods of electoral manipulation had been adopted, including attempts to reverse results in places where YSRCP candidates had won, he alleged.
He also accused Mr. Naidu of trying to divert attention from the alleged irregularities by raising questions about the local body elections held during the previous YSRCP regime.

Party leaders who attended the meeting reportedly described the recent elections as unprecedented in terms of irregularities and alleged that the State Election Commission had failed to ensure a free and fair electoral process.
They alleged that bouncers were deployed at counting centres in place of authorised election agents and that relatives of candidates were kidnapped to force them to withdraw their nominations.

The leaders further alleged that large numbers of votes polled in favour of YSRCP candidates were declared invalid during counting and that power supply was deliberately disrupted at some counting centres to facilitate manipulation.

They also complained that repeated recounting was ordered in constituencies where YSRCP candidates had secured victories, allegedly resulting in changes to the final tallies. However, requests for recounting made by YSRCP candidates were rejected, they said.

articles.title: Two days past Deepavali, NPCI yet to announce a date for UPI MDR rollout
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: About a month ago, when the NPCI had pushed back the rollout of MDR from its original date of October 15, it had said it would be implemented “immediately post Diwali”

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine hold second day of U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: ‘We are starting the second day of negotiations,’ Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, who leads Kyiv's delegation in Abu Dhabi, says on social media

Delegations from Moscow and Kyiv on Wednesday (November 11, 2026) held a second straight day of U.S.-brokered talks on ways of ending the war started by Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.

Hopes are low for any breakthrough in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations, although U.S. officials say they are determined to revive peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.
“We are starting the second day of negotiations,” Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv's delegation in Abu Dhabi, said on social media.

The envoys met for four hours on Tuesday (November 10) in the capital of the United Arab Emirates, which was chosen as a neutral venue. The talks, mediated by U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff, were due to conclude later Wednesday (November 11).

The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration has to reckon with Democrats, who could demand more support for Ukraine, taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections.
Also, Russia's wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.
Mr. Umerov said that Wednesday (November 11) would begin with three-way talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States, with Kyiv's delegation meeting afterwards with European officials.
Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations.
However, representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO were in Abu Dhabi and were consulting with the Ukrainian delegation, officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday's (November 10) session was “constructive and quite substantive”.

articles.title: Pakistan Deputy PM Ishaq Dar's grandson, seven others indicted in Lahore gang rape case
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: All the suspects, presently in judicial custody, were produced before the trial court for the indictment proceedings

A Pakistani court has indicted eight suspects, including the grandson of Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, in a gang rape of two foreign women, an official said on Wednesday (November 11, 2026).

"Lahore's Additional District & Sessions Judge (AD&SJ) Rafaqat Ali Gondal on Tuesday (November 10) framed charges against the suspects who pleaded not guilty," a court official said and added the judge directed the prosecution to present its witnesses on December 9 so that the formal trial proceedings could be commenced.
All the suspects, presently in judicial custody, were produced before the trial court for the indictment proceedings.
Ironically, Punjab police had already given a "clean chit" to Ishaq Dar's grandson Raza Dar and his four accomplices in this case.

Police not only absolved Dar's grandson and his four friends of rape charges but charged three other low-paid employees of him of raping the women, as per a police report earlier submitted in the court.

The two women, one from the Netherlands and the other from Venezuela, were allegedly kidnapped and raped by Raza Dar and four of his friends after arriving in Lahore on a business trip in June this year.
The medical examination confirmed that the foreign women were raped. Both victim women after recording their statements had left for their home countries.
According to the police report, the victim women said that they met Raza Dar in Singapore in 2025 and invited him to invest money with them in the business of crypto currency.
After getting profit returns on initial investment, Raza Dar invested over $500,000.

"However, this time, the women did not give any profit or return the amount to the suspect," the report said, adding in June this year, the suspect invited both women to Pakistan on the pretext of a meeting with another investor, where they stayed at a hotel in Islamabad and travelled to Murree hill station with their free will.

fullParagraphs: If anaemia reduction should align with India’s goals for NCD reduction, then the focus must be on better diets through diversification. That should be non-negotiable for public health policy: no amount of papering over cracks with pills and potions will work in the long term

India has had decades of unchanged high anaemia prevalence in women and children that has historically been thought to be due to iron deficiency. This has led firstly to an iron and folic acid (IFA) tablet supplementation targeted at women and children, and secondly to fitful implementation of mandatory fortification of staple foods. IFA is a ‘precision’ strategy, applying as it does to the vulnerable population it is intended for, while fortification is a broad strategy that applies to the entire population. The latter works in controlled settings such as clinical trials, but has not worked in real-world settings, and might have adverse effects when given to those it is unintended for.

The reason for pivoting: anaemia is mistakenly conflated with iron deficiency In India. The evidence is otherwise: in national Indian surveys, it has been shown that iron deficiency is not the major cause of anaemia. Indeed, fully one-third of anaemia cases demonstrate no micronutrient deficiency or obvious cause. Even so, giving iron should have sorted out those who did have iron deficiency anaemia, and reduced the general anaemia prevalence. While this could be a problem with inefficient programme implementation, two important questions arise: is there is really a deficiency in dietary iron intake in India? And is the administered iron being adequately absorbed and utilised for haemoglobin formation?

articles.title: Point of no return: On Israel’s next government
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Without peace, Israel risks descending into chaos

Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision to invite opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government reflects the real mandate of the October 27 legislative elections. While Mr. Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party finished second with 21 seats, behind Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud, which won 27, the former military chief, who campaigned on an anti-Netanyahu platform, has secured the support of 67 legislators in the 120-member Knesset. In Mr. Eisenkot’s own words, Israel risks “descending to dark places, to a point of no return”. But it is not yet clear what kind of a government Mr. Eisenkot is seeking to form. The opposition parties are split between a Jewish-led bloc with 48 MKs and an Arab-led bloc of 19 MKs. Arab parties have offered in-principle support for Mr. Eisenkot to keep Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition out of power. But what is not clear is whether they would be part of the government or offer outside support by allowing Mr. Eisenkot to run a minority government. Some of Mr. Eisenkot’s Jewish right-wing allies, such as Avigdor Lieberman, are opposed to joining hands with Arab parties. Mr. Eisenkot has now called for a unity government, appealing even to Likud and the far-right Religious Zionism, to join him.

But the challenges facing Israel’s next leader are formidable and immediate. Mr. Netanyahu’s unchecked militarism has deepened Israel’s international isolation, strained its relationship with the U.S., its most important patron and ally, and aggravated the security challenges it faces in its neighbourhood. At home, the surge of the far-right has further polarised society, while systemic violence against Palestinians has spread across the West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu’s response to these challenges has been to unleash more violence, which has only compounded Israel’s problems. If Mr. Eisenkot is serious about pulling Israel back from the point of no return, he must pursue a three-pronged approach. Firstly, he should form an Arab-Jewish unity government focused on healing the country’s internal wounds and bridging gaps between communities. Second, Israel’s deepening international isolation and increasingly negative public opinion around the world will begin to exact a heavy toll sooner rather than later. Tel Aviv must take urgent steps to restore its international standing. Third, Israel must reopen the path to peace. The new government should initiate negotiations with the Palestinians under international mediation, crack down on settler violence, pull back from Gaza and reaffirm its commitment to the two-state solution. Without peace, Israel risks continuing to “descend to dark places”.
Editorial Context: Point of no return: On Israel’s next government. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

• Without peace, Israel risks descending into chaos
• Israeli President Isaac Herzog’s decision to invite opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government reflects the real mandate of the October 27 legislative elections. While Mr. Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar party finished second with 21 seats, behind Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud, which won 27, the former military chief, who campaigned on an anti-Netanyahu platform, has secured the support of 67 legislators in the 120-member Knesset. In Mr. Eisenkot’s own words, Israel risks “descending to dark places, to a point of no return”. But it is not yet clear what kind of a government Mr. Eisenkot is seeking to form. The opposition parties are split between a Jewish-led bloc with 48 MKs and an Arab-led bloc of 19 MKs. Arab parties have offered in-principle support for Mr. Eisenkot to keep Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition out of power. Mr. Eisenkot has now called for a unity government, appealing even to Likud and the far-right Religious Zionism, to join him.
• But the challenges facing Israel’s next leader are formidable and immediate. Mr. Netanyahu’s unchecked militarism has deepened Israel’s international isolation, strained its relationship with the U.S., its most important patron and ally, and aggravated the security challenges it faces in its neighbourhood. At home, the surge of the far-right has further polarised society, while systemic violence against Palestinians has spread across the West Bank. Mr. Netanyahu’s response to these challenges has been to unleash more violence, which has only compounded Israel’s problems. If Mr. Eisenkot is serious about pulling Israel back from the point of no return, he must pursue a three-pronged approach. Firstly, he should form an Arab-Jewish unity government focused on healing the country’s internal wounds and bridging gaps between communities. Second, Israel’s deepening international isolation and increasingly negative public opinion around the world will begin to exact a heavy toll sooner rather than later. Tel Aviv must take urgent steps to restore its international standing. Third, Israel must reopen the path to peace. The new government should initiate negotiations with the Palestinians under international mediation, crack down on settler violence, pull back from Gaza and reaffirm its commitment to the two-state solution. Without peace, Israel risks continuing to “descend to dark places”.

fullParagraphs: As F1’s youngest champion, Kimi Antonelli can attract a new generation of fans

Andrea Kimi Antonelli etched his name in motorsport history by becoming the youngest driver to win a Formula One World Championship . The 20-year-old has secured his maiden title with four races to spare after finishing third at the Mexico Grand Prix on Sunday. The Italian’s feat is remarkable, for he has claimed the crown in his sophomore campaign, becoming only the fifth driver in history to do so in the first or second season. Mercedes signed Antonelli for its junior driver programme when he was just 12. Since then, the Italian’s step towards F1 has been meticulously managed. After acing the F4 championships, Antonelli skipped one level to transition to F2. And when the opportunity arose to fill a seat vacated by seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes boss Toto Wolff took a bold gamble by drafting in the youngster. Antonelli’s rookie campaign in 2025 was baptism by fire, and he was outclassed by teammate George Russell. For 2026, F1 ushered in drastic changes with new engine and aerodynamic regulations, dramatically altering the dynamics of the cars. Though conventional wisdom suggested that the experienced Russell would be the favourite, the Italian prodigy embraced the challenge astonishingly well. This was best exemplified by how he won five consecutive races starting from the second round of the season.

One of the hardest things in F1 is handling the nerves associated with protecting the lead, especially when it is the driver’s first attempt at a Championship bid. Antonelli, though, was incredibly consistent throughout the year, and hardly made any errors. Titles are often decided by how a driver minimises his losses on bad days, and Antonelli showed great temperament in this regard. At the same time, he was ruthless on the track and made decisive overtaking manoeuvres. The defining race was in Monza, Italy, in September, where Antonelli charged from 19th on the grid to win his home Grand Prix, finishing ahead of Russell who started second. It was a statement of intent, and strengthened his grip on the trophy. Drivers often raise their games following a world title, more so when success comes early in their career. The charm of the sport lies in its iconic driver rivalries such as Ayrton Senna versus Alain Prost, and Michael Schumacher versus Mika Hakkinen. With four-time champion Max Verstappen widely considered the gold standard of the present era, Antonelli could well be the perfect candidate to battle the Dutchman in F1’s next great rivalry.

articles.title: Epic failures: on electoral roll, welfare
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: The electoral roll cannot be used to determine welfare beneficiaries

Union Panchayati Raj Minister Rajiv Ranjan Singh’s statement that voter identity cards, with biometric authentication, will replace Aadhaar as the basis for identifying beneficiaries and making payments under his Ministry’s schemes runs contrary to existing laws and regulations. Essentially, the electoral roll, prepared in several States through the flawed Special Intensive Revision (SIR) by the Election Commission of India (ECI), will become the dataset to vet the identities of beneficiaries. This contradicts the Supreme Court’s May 27 judgment on the Bihar SIR and its observations while hearing petitions against West Bengal’s orders removing people deleted during the SIR from the Public Distribution System and the Annapurna Yojana. The Court held that the ECI may undertake only a “limited enquiry” into citizenship to decide who belongs on the electoral roll, and that “any action taken pursuant thereto is confined to electoral consequences alone”. The consequence of deletion from the rolls, it said, is “correspondingly limited” to a person’s place on the roll and their right to vote. The Court also called the EPIC “a derivative document, issued on the basis of inclusion in the electoral roll”, and held that relying on it to verify that very roll would defeat the exercise. It is ironic that Mr. Singh now wants this “derivative document” to be the determinant of welfare benefits.

Not every citizen is an eligible voter, and tying benefits to the electoral roll is illogical and also cruel. In West Bengal, lakhs were deleted from the rolls , many for dubious “logical discrepancies”. In the appeals heard for reinstatement, 93% resulted in the restoration of names by September 2026, pointing to massive pre-election disenfranchisement. The Court has stated that it is yet to adjudicate on the legality of the ECI’s “logical discrepancies” method. The SIR was designed by the ECI to restrict enrolment through stringent residency criteria; thus, itinerant voters had to prove their eligibility. The Opposition, civil society and even some of the BJP’s allies have objected to this, but the BJP refuses to acknowledge the SIR’s flaws. This is partly because it has benefited from disenfranchisement — as in West Bengal. But the Minister’s remarks suggest another reason. The BJP-led coalition sees the pruned electoral rolls as a way to limit welfare, especially at a time when growth in tax revenues has slowed because of the Centre’s policies. Inordinately delaying the Census, changing the procedure to appoint Election Commissioners, who then run an exercise that disenfranchises millions by design, and now, using the resultant rolls to decide who gets welfare, all cut at the heart of the painstakingly built constitutional welfare state. The sooner the Court decides the petitions against the SIR, and reiterates that its rolls cannot be used to curtail welfare, the better.

Union Panchayati Raj Minister Rajiv Ranjan Singh’s statement that voter identity cards, with biometric authentication, will replace Aadhaar as the basis for identifying beneficiaries and making payments under his Ministry’s schemes runs contrary to existing laws and regulations. Essentially, the electoral roll, prepared in several States through the flawed Special Intensive Revision (SIR) by the Election Commission of India (ECI), will become the dataset to vet the identities of beneficiaries. This contradicts the Supreme Court’s May 27 judgment on the Bihar SIR and its observations while hearing petitions against West Bengal’s orders removing people deleted during the SIR from the Public Distribution System and the Annapurna Yojana. The Court held that the ECI may undertake only a “limited enquiry” into citizenship to decide who belongs on the electoral roll, and that “any action taken pursuant thereto is confined to electoral consequences alone”. The consequence of deletion from the rolls, it said, is “correspondingly limited” to a person’s place on the roll and their right to vote. The Court also called the EPIC “a derivative document, issued on the basis of inclusion in the electoral roll”, and held that relying on it to verify that very roll would defeat the exercise. It is ironic that Mr. Singh now wants this “derivative document” to be the determinant of welfare benefits.

Not every citizen is an eligible voter, and tying benefits to the electoral roll is illogical and also cruel. In West Bengal, lakhs were deleted from the rolls , many for dubious “logical discrepancies”. In the appeals heard for reinstatement, 93% resulted in the restoration of names by September 2026, pointing to massive pre-election disenfranchisement. The Court has stated that it is yet to adjudicate on the legality of the ECI’s “logical discrepancies” method. The SIR was designed by the ECI to restrict enrolment through stringent residency criteria; thus, itinerant voters had to prove their eligibility. The Opposition, civil society and even some of the BJP’s allies have objected to this, but the BJP refuses to acknowledge the SIR’s flaws. This is partly because it has benefited from disenfranchisement — as in West Bengal. But the Minister’s remarks suggest another reason. The BJP-led coalition sees the pruned electoral rolls as a way to limit welfare, especially at a time when growth in tax revenues has slowed because of the Centre’s policies. Inordinately delaying the Census, changing the procedure to appoint Election Commissioners, who then run an exercise that disenfranchises millions by design, and now, using the resultant rolls to decide who gets welfare, all cut at the heart of the painstakingly built constitutional welfare state. The sooner the Court decides the petitions against the SIR, and reiterates that its rolls cannot be used to curtail welfare, the better.

articles.title: Trump debacle: On the U.S. midterm election results
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Democrats must use their win to influence policy and improve lives

President Donald Trump faced the worst political setback of his current term in office after the Republican Party lost control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives in the mid-term election. Democrats not only won resoundingly in their traditional stronghold States, such as Colorado, Oregon and Illinois, and held onto important swing States, such as Georgia, Michigan and Virginia, but they also made historic inroads into “red states” such as Texas, Kansas and Iowa. While Mr. Trump fumed that Republicans would have performed better had his name been on the ballot, he also appeared to be resigned to the imminent reality of working with Democratic lawmakers over the remaining two years of his administration. Beyond the immediate impact on the future functioning of the federal government, this week’s “bluenami” has also brought sweeping changes at the State level: Democrats won a Senate seat in Texas for the first time in 37 years; Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan , making him the first Muslim Senator in history ; Chris Pappas of New Hampshire became the first openly gay man to be elected to the Senate ; and Senate Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries will soon be the first African-American Speaker of the House.
Federal judge orders 14-day delay on any work beginning on Trump’s monumental arch

It is ironic that Mr. Trump alluded to his name not being on the ballot as the cause for the Republican collapse because, for many voters, the midterm election was indeed a referendum on the second Trump administration’s performance in office. The result has been an unambiguous thumbs-down from voters so far as top policy areas of the Trump administration are concerned, including cost of living and jobs, immigration enforcement, the war in Iran. The writing was on the wall, as were the approval ratings, especially in the case of oil prices and the Iran war, given that the price of gas in the U.S. has soared since the conflict around the Strait of Hormuz escalated. Similarly, the widespread raids by ICE and accelerated deportation processes for undocumented migrants led to protests across States and galvanised progressives around immigration reform. While Democrats may be justified in celebrating their victory after two years of harsh Trumpism, they would do well to remember that the President still retains a veto vote for policies passed by Congress. The temptation to launch a series of investigations and interrogate the functioning of the Trump White House may be strong, yet congressional Democrats may wish to avoid any posturing that yields no palpable policy impact, including kicking off impeachment proceedings against Mr. Trump. A more productive way forward for Democratic lawmakers would be to engage with the White House and, through negotiation and compromise, mitigate the real impact of deleterious policies in critical areas such as health-care insurance and tariffs.

articles.title: Danger in the sewer: On India’s sewer cleaning deaths
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: India must eliminate situations that lead to sewer cleaning deaths

Despite legislation, Supreme Court orders, government programmes, the availability of mechanised cleaning technologies, and exhortations from politicians, India continues to lose sanitation workers to foreseeable, and largely preventable, circumstances. In a recent incident, four workers lost their lives in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh , cleaning a hotel’s food-waste chamber. According to Parliament and the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis data, the number of workers who died on jobs involving sewer and septic tanks was 859 between 2014 and 2025, 498 from 2019 to mid-2026, 332 across 18 States and Union Territories in 2021-26, and 1,350 between 1993 and 2025. The figures have never tended towards zero even as the Safai Karamchari Andolan has repeatedly alleged severe under-reporting. Further, the government has maintained since at least 2021 that the practice of manually cleaning excreta from insanitary latrines has been eliminated, effectively signalling that it believes it has addressed the root of the problem when it has not, and freeing administrative bodies of the urgency of inspecting municipalities and private establishments. Members of historically marginalised castes are also overrepresented in these jobs. The law has distinguished hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks from manual scavenging since 2013. Even so, persons entering them are still vulnerable to noxious gases. In Dr. Balram Singh (2023), the Court strengthened the requirements under Safai Karamchari Andolan (2014) to, among other measures, ensure outsourced sewer-cleaning contracts did not entail workers entering sewers and raise the compensation for deaths to ₹30 lakh per worker. In 2025, there was an order to end manual sewer cleaning in four metropolitan cities, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad followed a year later with notices to 15 Chief Secretaries for disobeying the 2023 order, including on the compensation.

Private contractors and municipal bodies are known to violate the restrictions on manual cleaning specified in the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act 2013 and Rules, and evade liability by hiring undocumented daily-wage workers. The scourge of such worker deaths thus cannot be eliminated without also formalising their employment and improving social security across caste lines. A significant gap between aims and outcomes has also persisted under the National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem scheme . And while it is centred on urban local bodies, its difficulties speak to the state’s fundamental error: to maximise administrative assistance, such as by distributing kits, rather than minimising the number of situations that could lead to worker deaths.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 10 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 3 Min Read

📰 Danger in the sewer: On India’s sewer cleaning deaths

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

India must eliminate situations that lead to sewer cleaning deaths

Despite legislation, Supreme Court orders, government programmes, the availability of mechanised cleaning technologies, and exhortations from politicians, India continues to lose sanitation workers to foreseeable, and largely preventable, circumstances. In a recent incident, four workers lost their lives in Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh , cleaning a hotel’s food-waste chamber. According to Parliament and the National Commission for Safai Karamcharis data, the number of workers who died on jobs involving sewer and septic tanks was 859 between 2014 and 2025, 498 from 2019 to mid-2026, 332 across 18 States and Union Territories in 2021-26, and 1,350 between 1993 and 2025. The figures have never tended towards zero even as the Safai Karamchari Andolan has repeatedly alleged severe under-reporting. Further, the government has maintained since at least 2021 that the practice of manually cleaning excreta from insanitary latrines has been eliminated, effectively signalling that it believes it has addressed the root of the problem when it has not, and freeing administrative bodies of the urgency of inspecting municipalities and private establishments. Members of historically marginalised castes are also overrepresented in these jobs. The law has distinguished hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks from manual scavenging since 2013. Even so, persons entering them are still vulnerable to noxious gases. In Dr. Balram Singh (2023), the Court strengthened the requirements under Safai Karamchari Andolan (2014) to, among other measures, ensure outsourced sewer-cleaning contracts did not entail workers entering sewers and raise the compensation for deaths to ₹30 lakh per worker. In 2025, there was an order to end manual sewer cleaning in four metropolitan cities, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad followed a year later with notices to 15 Chief Secretaries for disobeying the 2023 order, including on the compensation.

Private contractors and municipal bodies are known to violate the restrictions on manual cleaning specified in the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act 2013 and Rules, and evade liability by hiring undocumented daily-wage workers. The scourge of such worker deaths thus cannot be eliminated without also formalising their employment and improving social security across caste lines. A significant gap between aims and outcomes has also persisted under the National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem scheme . And while it is centred on urban local bodies, its difficulties speak to the state’s fundamental error: to maximise administrative assistance, such as by distributing kits, rather than minimising the number of situations that could lead to worker deaths.

articles.title: Slow recovery: On the ISRO’s GSLV-F18 mission
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: ISRO needs more human and material resources to fulfil its mandate

With the successful launch of the GSLV-F18 mission and the NVS-03 satellite’s healthy status , the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is on course to heave a sigh of relief. Its last 18 months have been constrained by the consequences of two launch failures involving PSLV rockets , which share some of their design aspects with GSLV, to the extent that the F18 mission was only the second successful launch of 2026. If the NVS-03 satellite is successfully manoeuvred into its final intended orbital slot and commissioned, ISRO will also have pulled off a rescue mission for the ‘Navigation with Indian Constellation’ (NavIC) programme , which has been at least one functional satellite short for the last six months and thus unable to meet its primary purpose of providing standalone positioning services over the Indian subcontinent. The three second-generation NVS satellites thus far are distinguished by having at least one indigenously made atomic clock onboard, in line with the recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee (PSC) on Science and Technology and India’s investments in quantum timekeeping, and away from the imported clocks onboard the first-generation IRNSS satellites.

The PSC had also flagged procurement bottlenecks across ISRO’s programmes, including difficulties with obtaining specialised components and ensuring vendor readiness on the timelines that NavIC needs. The ISRO Space Applications Centre’s ‘request for proposals’ in 2025 also specified a large lead time of nearly two years between a contract’s start and the first two flight models. The Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme and the programme to modernise the Semiconductor Laboratory can be tweaked to serve these needs, with the Electronics Ministry also setting aside dedicated funds for developing specialised components and their qualification tests in a five- to seven-year programme. In tandem, the government must allocate around ₹17,000 crore in the 2027-28 Union Budget for the Department of Space, against ₹13,705.6 crore in 2026-27, with the hike focusing on manufacturing launch vehicles, replacing satellites, and recruitment. Besides, NavIC also requires a dedicated operator, so that ISRO can be left to focus on its core mandate, and India needs a national space law addressing private participation in this enterprise, and liability. Two successful orbital missions in five-sixths of a year is unbecoming of a national space programme with imminent plans of human spaceflight, a space station, and reusable launch vehicle capabilities. Without significant measures, ISRO will lurch from one mission to the next as and when its inadequate workforce is able to make do with its inadequate allocation.

articles.title: Building over Srinagar’s future
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Suspend the FAR and land-use exemptions, along with Section 22, until they are brought within the Master Plan framework and subjected to public objections

Two conversations about the Himalayas are running at the same time, and they are not converging. Everyone agrees that mountain towns are reaching their limits in different ways, springs are drying up, lakes are choking, and slopes are giving way. No hill town should approve large construction before measuring what it can carry. Yet the developmental model is running parallel. Recent notifications and bills in Jammu and Kashmir are making it easier to build more, on more land. Srinagar is being overwhelmed by that.

Let us start with a simple idea. Floor Area Ratio (FAR) determines how much floor space can be built on a plot. On a 100-square-metre plot, an FAR of 200% allows 200 square metres of floor space. When the number is raised, the same plot must hold more people, cars, toilets, drains, etc. Over nine months, the rules have been repeatedly changed. The building by-laws were amended on December 1, 2025. On July 24, 2026, they were extended to Housing Board colonies, with additional FAR and reduced setbacks. On September 9, fresh limits were proposed, including an FAR of 300% for commercial complexes. On September 28, the Ease of Doing Business Bill, 2026, was tabled. In the first week of October, the Lieutenant Governor gave his assent, and the Bill became law.
Political & National Report: Building over Srinagar’s future. This development is a key milestone in India's ongoing legislative, judicial, and constitutional governance framework.

Suspend the FAR and land-use exemptions, along with Section 22, until they are brought within the Master Plan framework and subjected to public objections

Two conversations about the Himalayas are running at the same time, and they are not converging. Everyone agrees that mountain towns are reaching their limits in different ways, springs are drying up, lakes are choking, and slopes are giving way. No hill town should approve large construction before measuring what it can carry. Yet the developmental model is running parallel. Recent notifications and bills in Jammu and Kashmir are making it easier to build more, on more land. Srinagar is being overwhelmed by that.

Let us start with a simple idea. Floor Area Ratio (FAR) determines how much floor space can be built on a plot. On a 100-square-metre plot, an FAR of 200% allows 200 square metres of floor space. When the number is raised, the same plot must hold more people, cars, toilets, drains, etc. Over nine months, the rules have been repeatedly changed. The building by-laws were amended on December 1, 2025. On July 24, 2026, they were extended to Housing Board colonies, with additional FAR and reduced setbacks. On September 9, fresh limits were proposed, including an FAR of 300% for commercial complexes. On September 28, the Ease of Doing Business Bill, 2026, was tabled. In the first week of October, the Lieutenant Governor gave his assent, and the Bill became law.

articles.title: Wayanad conservationist N. Badusha wins environmental award
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Wayanad Prakruthi Samrakshana Samithi (WPSS) president N. Badusha has been selected for the seventh environmental award instituted by the Dr. Kamarudeen Foundation for Biodiversity Conservation (KFBC).

The award, instituted in memory of Kamarudeen, a noted environmentalist and former Reader in the Department of Botany at the University of Kerala, carries a cash prize of ₹25,000, a citation, and a plaque.
Mr. Badusha, a conservationist, is known for his efforts to protect Wayanad’s ecology and ecological heritage.

KFBC officials said this year's award was intended to recognise selfless environmental activists who had made exemplary contributions to biodiversity conservation and enhancement through their own efforts, without relying on government support or official facilities. In recognition of his contributions, Mr. Badusha was unanimously selected for the 2026 award, they said.
The award will be presented in a function to be held at Kariavattom in Thiruvananthapuram on November 13.

articles.title: At peak of air pollution on Deepavali, data goes missing at several government monitoring stations in Delhi
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Missing PM2.5 data for several hours on CPCB website understated city’s pollution levels: experts; 227 PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 stations; govt. will look into it: Mishra

Air quality data from several government monitoring stations in Delhi went missing for hours during the pollution spike following Deepavali on Sunday (November 8, 2026), with experts warning that the gaps have led to understated pollution levels and resulted in a lower official air quality index (AQI).

According to Dr. D. Saha, former head of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)’s air quality laboratory, AQI values are calculated using a moving or running average of hourly concentrations of eight parameters, including PM2.5 and PM10, over the previous 24 hours.

On Monday (November 9, 2026), PM2.5 data were missing for several hours at many stations in the city, including Anand Vihar, Patparganj and Bawana, on the CPCB website. PM2.5 (particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter) consists of fine inhalable particles that can penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream, causing respiratory and other diseases. Similar data gaps were reported at several monitoring stations during Deepavali last year as well.

Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finland-based non-profit research organisation, said the missing hourly PM2.5 data “raised concerns about the assessment of Delhi’s air quality”.

“From midnight on November 8 until 5 a.m. on November 9, 227 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation,” Mr. Kumar said, adding, “When the hourly PM2.5 data is missing, it will artificially lower the AQI, showing better air quality when the actual air quality is worse.”

When asked about the missing air quality data at several monitoring stations, Delhi Labour Minister Kapil Mishra told the media that the government would look into the issue. The Member Secretary of the CPCB, which releases AQI data, did not respond to calls and messages seeking comment.
Dr. Saha told The Hindu that there should not be gaps in the data, especially during crucial periods.

“If hourly PM2.5 or PM10 value is blank or missing, it will affect the AQI calculated and the final value of the AQI calculated will be less than the actual value of AQI and scientifically incorrect,” Mr. Saha said.

He also said the CPCB had set the measurement range of PM2.5 analysers at 0–1,000 micrograms per cubic metre, which meant they could not measure concentrations above that level. “So, if the value of PM2.5 is beyond 1,000, it should at least be shown as 1,000 instead of showing blank,” he said.

A former DPCC scientist, who did not wish to be identified, said the CPCB recorded PM2.5 values only up to 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre because there was a minor drop in accuracy at higher levels. “But at very high values, a small drop in accuracy will not matter a lot. Ideally, the CPCB should be measuring the higher values so that we are not missing the peak values,” the official said, adding that not measuring higher concentrations would artificially make air quality appear better.

fullParagraphs: India is ready to mediate to establish grain safety agreement for “food corridors”, says Ukrainian President Zelenskyy

India is ready to mediate between Russia and Ukraine to establish “food corridors”, announced Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, welcoming the offer after a telephone call with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, ahead of the Ukraine-Russia peace talks set to begin in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday. Mr. Modi conveyed India’s “readiness” to help with all initiatives to end the nearly five-year-old conflict. The call was followed by another call between External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, in the clearest indication thus far of the mediatory role that New Delhi is now playing between Moscow and Kyiv.

On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump’s negotiators, including his son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, will restart negotiations after three months with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to discuss security guarantees required for a possible ceasefire. The calls from New Delhi came just ahead of the talks in the UAE, and a week before Mr. Modi and Mr. Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the ASEAN-linked summits in Manila. Later this month, Mr. Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen for the APEC summit in China, that Russian President Vladimir Putin is also expected to attend, making the timing of the Modi-Zelenskyy and Jaishankar-Lavrov calls more significant.

“Prime Minister [Modi] reaffirmed India’s human-centric approach and reiterated India’s consistent position that the conflict must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy,” the Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement about the Modi-Zelenskyy call. “He conveyed India’s readiness to contribute to all efforts aimed at peaceful resolution of the conflict,” it added.

In a post on social media, Mr. Zelenskyy said he had briefed Mr. Modi on the latest developments and stressed that Mr. Modi had said to Mr. Putin that the war must end. The Ukrainian President said Russia must understand that the “global economy and hundreds of millions of people around the world are suffering because of blocked sea routes” in the Black Sea, and called for India to clarify its peace proposal.

“It is important that India identify what steps it can take and what dialogue it can pursue with other leaders to help bring the war to an end. Food security could be one such area. We discussed Russia’s blocking of grain exports via the Black Sea. India is ready to mediate in establishing food corridors, and we are counting on these efforts to continue,” Mr. Zelenskyy wrote.

Within a couple of hours of the announcement, Mr. Jaishankar posted that he had spoken to his Russian counterpart Mr. Lavrov as well, and said their conversation had “focused on the Ukraine conflict and ongoing diplomatic initiatives”. Mr. Jaishankar, who has been discussing India’s proposals on a grain export agreement or a food corridor in the Black Sea, on the safety of sea mariners, and safe passage for energy shipments with both countries, had first disclosed the initiatives during a visit to Poland and Ukraine in September. On October 22, during the visit of Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to Delhi, Indian officials had said it had reached out to both Russian and Ukrainian governments with a “four-point proposal” for an agreement that would stop attacks on civilians, allow grain and energy exports from both countries through the Black Sea, and end the targeting of ships and seafarers, many of whom are Indian nationals. Highly placed officials had told The Hindu that New Delhi was in close contact with both sides over the specific proposal, and the government had hoped to hear back from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides at the earliest. With talks set to begin on Tuesday, it remains to be seen whether India will join the dialogue already in play with the U.S. and the UAE, or whether New Delhi plans a larger role in mediating or hosting talks between Russia and Ukraine in the future.

articles.title: Five persons, including four girls, drown in irrigation tank in Tiruvannamalai
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The deceased were identified as a staff nurse and four inmates of a government-recognised children’s home for girls
A staff nurse and four girls of a government-recognised children’s home for girls drowned in an irrigation tank at Samuthiram village here on Monday (November 9, 2026).

The deceased were identified as staff nurse Thenmozhi, 24, Vijayalakshmi, 14, Alli, 14, Poomika, 13, and Valliammal, 16. Except Valliammal, who belongs to Kilpennathur village, the other three girls are siblings from Karapattu village near Chengam. The deceased did not know swimming, the police said. Initial inquiry revealed the home had been functioning for over a decade in the area.

On Monday afternoon, Thenmozhi, along with around 13 girls, went to the irrigation tank on Perumbakkam Main Road to bathe. Poomika and her siblings and Valliammal stepped into the water and slipped and fell into a deeper portion of the irrigation tank. The police said Thenmozhi tried to save the children but also drowned.

Hearing the other girls’ shouts, the area’s residents rushed to the spot and alerted the Tiruvannamalai West police and firefighters. Firefighters retrieved the bodies and sent them to the Government Medical College and Hospital in Tiruvannamalai town for a post-mortem. A case has been registered.

Collector Vandhana Garg and Superintendent of Police R. Uthayakumar met the families of the deceased at the hospital in the presence of hospital dean Edvina Vasantah and inspected the irrigation tank. A probe is under way.

articles.title: From poverty alleviation to prosperity

fullParagraphs: India has reduced extreme poverty, but its high prosperity gap shows that millions remain far from a comfortable standard of living; informal work, stagnant wages and limited employment opportunities continue to constrain upward mobility

From the poverty income ruler line provided by the recent World Bank estimates, India has recorded one of the fastest extreme income-poverty declines in the world, as per its latest Poverty and Equity brief, which highlights that between 2011 and 2023, an estimated 496 million people moved out of poverty, with extreme income-based poverty ($3/per day) declining to 2.6%.

For the same period, the share of the population living below the lower middle-income country line ($4.20/day, 2021 PPP) fell from 57.7% to 16.1%. Non-monetary poverty indicators, as per OPHI’s Multi-dimensional Poverty Index, also recorded a sharp reduction in overall poverty numbers, i.e., from 53.8% in 2005-06 to 16.4% in 2019-21.

articles.title: Rampur’s Lavi Fair: Storytelling through 300 years of Himalayan trade and tradition
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Rampur Bushahr’s Lavi Fair in Himachal Pradesh traces a Himalayan journey from wool and barter to women entrepreneurs and digital payments

What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

For a few weeks, Rampur, on the banks of the Sutlej river, comes alive with the fair (November 11-14 this year, with trading grounds open through the month), offering a sensory map of the Himalaya. Colourful textiles, yak wool, pashmina, dry fruits, agricultural produce, Kinnauri apples, indigenous crafts and precious stones fill the marketplace. Among its most captivating sights are the magnificent Chamurthi horses, the hardy “ships of the cold desert”.
Kinnauri weaves on sale at Lavi Fair. | Photo Credit: Nitika Kuthiala
At the Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, Shimla district. | Photo Credit: Nitika Kuthiala
Jewellery on sale at Lavi Fair. | Photo Credit: Nitika Kuthiala

Traders once travelled from Tibet, Nepal, Central Asia and Afghanistan. Tradition traces the fair’s origins to a 17th-century treaty between Raja Kehri Singh of Bushahr and Tibet, establishing it as a meeting point for traders, pilgrims and storytellers along the Silk Route. Though trans-Himalayan trade declined after Tibet’s occupation in 1959, the fair survived on the Buddhist circuit and was accorded international status by the Himachal Pradesh government.

Pratibha Singh, a member of the Rampur Bushahr royal family which founded the fair and continues to honour the tradition, recalls its legacy of pashmina and Kinnauri shawls, some woven over years, alongside trans-Himalayan textiles and local produce. Rampur Bushahr’s Lavi Fair in Himachal Pradesh traces a Himalayan journey from wool and barter to women entrepreneurs and digital payments

What Disneyland is to children today, Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, in Himachal Pradesh’s Shimla district, was to my family in the 1980s. I recall wandering through the fair as an eight-year-old, watching an old man smoking a chillum beside heaps of black sheep fleece and stacks of white woollen pattus (traditional garments of Kinnaur and Kullu women).

Mother and her friends carefully chose shawls for their daughters’ and future daughters-in-law’s trousseaux. Years later, I received a beautiful black sheep wool and pashmina shawl for my wedding. Wool finds pride of place at the fair. The name Lavi is linked to “Loe”, a sheet of woollen cloth and the practice of shearing sheep.

For a few weeks, Rampur, on the banks of the Sutlej river, comes alive with the fair (November 11-14 this year, with trading grounds open through the month), offering a sensory map of the Himalaya. Colourful textiles, yak wool, pashmina, dry fruits, agricultural produce, Kinnauri apples, indigenous crafts and precious stones fill the marketplace. Among its most captivating sights are the magnificent Chamurthi horses, the hardy “ships of the cold desert”.

Kinnauri weaves on sale at Lavi Fair. | Photo Credit: Nitika Kuthiala

At the Lavi Fair in Rampur Bushahr, Shimla district. | Photo Credit: Nitika Kuthiala

Jewellery on sale at Lavi Fair. | Photo Credit: Nitika Kuthiala

Traders once travelled from Tibet, Nepal, Central Asia and Afghanistan. Tradition traces the fair’s origins to a 17th-century treaty between Raja Kehri Singh of Bushahr and Tibet, establishing it as a meeting point for traders, pilgrims and storytellers along the Silk Route. Though trans-Himalayan trade declined after Tibet’s occupation in 1959, the fair survived on the Buddhist circuit and was accorded international status by the Himachal Pradesh government.

Pratibha Singh, a member of the Rampur Bushahr royal family which founded the fair and continues to honour the tradition, recalls its legacy of pashmina and Kinnauri shawls, some woven over years, alongside trans-Himalayan textiles and local produce. The GI-tagged Kinnauri shawl, with bright geometric motifs, speaks its own language of colour: white for water, yellow for earth, red for fire, green for air, and blue for sky.

On my last visit, a group of elderly women from South India told me they discovered the fair through a fellow traveller whose husband was a biker in the 1990s. A friend from Odisha recalls how in the 90s, his ophthalmologist-father’s eye camps in Rampur led to lifelong friendships and an annual habit of sourcing Kinnauri apples and dry fruits.

Kinnauri apples on sale at Lavi Fair. | Photo Credit: Nitika Kuthiala

articles.title: Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Any regulation of crackers needs strict enforcement at all levels

The two Deepavali nights following the Supreme Court’s (SC) temporary relaxation of the cracker ban , played out predictably. The Air Quality Index (AQI) in several north Indian cities — already ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ in the first week of November — was ‘severe’ on Deepavali night . Several air sensors — maintained by various organisations — reported PM2.5 in Delhi and its outskirts, exceeding 1,000 by Deepavali night. In this context, the SC’s order last week regarding crackers bears revisiting. While stating it was aware of the consequences of emissions from crackers, the Court has been waiting for quantitative evidence on the health and environmental effects of emissions from Deepavali celebrations. Such direct, causative evidence is almost impossible to furnish. Slackening winds and post-monsoon atmospheric dryness are known to trap the latent particulate matter from vehicles, industries, construction dust and stubble burning. Crackers are only an additional element that further degrades an already vitiated air. Delhi’s five-day average AQI rose from approximately 298 before Deepavali to 358 afterwards in 2024, 259 to 315 in 2025 and from 350 to 376 in 2026. While the timing of these spikes is consistent with a contribution from firecrackers, their precise share of overall pollution cannot be isolated from other emissions and meteorological influences. An absolute ban would encourage “illegal crackers from across the border,” the Court was told. Cracker season begins a fortnight before Deepavali and therefore an earlier decision by the Court regarding its permissibility would have given stockists time to better dispense ‘green’ crackers.

However, it is important to note that CSIR-NEERI, the developers of the products, underline that low-emission crackers — under stringent lab conditions — only reduce emissions by 30%–45%. These percentage reductions reveal nothing about gross particulate matter emissions. The post-Deepavali AQI is evidence of this. The Court acknowledges, but does not address, the immense implementation challenges in policing cracker sales and hyphenates crackers with religious observation but pays only lip service to provisions in the Constitution that say that religious customs cannot override considerations of health and life. Rather than wait for the week running up to Deepavali 2027, the Court must pronounce a final view on crackers and lay down the contours for the government to evolve a policy on limiting the manufacture, sale, and burning of crackers in a time-bound manner.

Editorial Context: Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban. This editorial examines the institutional, constitutional, and pragmatic dimensions shaping public policy and governance in India.

✍️ Editorial & Opinion 📅 10 Nov 2026 ⏱️ 3 Min Read

📰 Cracker conundrum: On need for strict enforcement of cracker ban

🎯 Exam Relevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions

Any regulation of crackers needs strict enforcement at all levels

The two Deepavali nights following the Supreme Court’s (SC) temporary relaxation of the cracker ban , played out predictably. The Air Quality Index (AQI) in several north Indian cities — already ‘poor’ and ‘very poor’ in the first week of November — was ‘severe’ on Deepavali night . Several air sensors — maintained by various organisations — reported PM2.5 in Delhi and its outskirts, exceeding 1,000 by Deepavali night. In this context, the SC’s order last week regarding crackers bears revisiting. While stating it was aware of the consequences of emissions from crackers, the Court has been waiting for quantitative evidence on the health and environmental effects of emissions from Deepavali celebrations. Such direct, causative evidence is almost impossible to furnish. Slackening winds and post-monsoon atmospheric dryness are known to trap the latent particulate matter from vehicles, industries, construction dust and stubble burning. Crackers are only an additional element that further degrades an already vitiated air. Delhi’s five-day average AQI rose from approximately 298 before Deepavali to 358 afterwards in 2024, 259 to 315 in 2025 and from 350 to 376 in 2026. While the timing of these spikes is consistent with a contribution from firecrackers, their precise share of overall pollution cannot be isolated from other emissions and meteorological influences. An absolute ban would encourage “illegal crackers from across the border,” the Court was told. Cracker season begins a fortnight before Deepavali and therefore an earlier decision by the Court regarding its permissibility would have given stockists time to better dispense ‘green’ crackers.

However, it is important to note that CSIR-NEERI, the developers of the products, underline that low-emission crackers — under stringent lab conditions — only reduce emissions by 30%–45%. These percentage reductions reveal nothing about gross particulate matter emissions. The post-Deepavali AQI is evidence of this. The Court acknowledges, but does not address, the immense implementation challenges in policing cracker sales and hyphenates crackers with religious observation but pays only lip service to provisions in the Constitution that say that religious customs cannot override considerations of health and life. Rather than wait for the week running up to Deepavali 2027, the Court must pronounce a final view on crackers and lay down the contours for the government to evolve a policy on limiting the manufacture, sale, and burning of crackers in a time-bound manner.

articles.title: Postpone panchayat, municipal elections to April-May next year: Ladakh group
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: “We suspect that this government is up to some mischief. We saw ‘vote chori’ in West Bengal, Bihar, Haryana, Maharashtra etc. In entire India 13 crore voters were dropped from the voter list. Ladakh is a small region and fraud is easy,” said Ladakh Buddhist Association (LBA) chairman Tsering Dorjey Lakrook

Several groups in Ladakh on Monday (November 9, 2026) demanded postponement of panchayat and municipal elections and alleged the authorities were up to some mischief in the region, which saw street agitation over the demands of Statehood and Sixth Schedule in the past six years. Meanwhile, a shutdown call has been issued in Kargil over the election.

“We suspect that this government is up to some mischief. We saw ‘vote chori’ in West Bengal, Bihar, Haryana, Maharashtra etc. In entire India 13 crore voters were dropped from the voter list. Ladakh is a small region and fraud is easy,” said Ladakh Buddhist Association (LBA) chairman Tsering Dorjey Lakrook.

Terming the upcoming panchayat and municipal elections as “conspiracy against people of Ladakh”, Mr. Lakrook, who is also co-chairman of the Leh Apex Body (LAB), said, “I warn people of Ladakh that these elections are a conspiracy. People of Ladakh should stay awake. We demand postponement of these elections. Let the authorities first frame the constituencies and hold the election in April-May next year,” said Mr. Lakrook.

The Lieutenant Governor administration of Ladakh last month dissolved the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council (LAHDC)-Kargil and announced panchayat and municipal elections on November 21 and the process shall be completed before November 30, officials said.
“The back-to-back elections are held in a hurry. These elections will see greater participation if held next year,” said Mr. Lakrook.
Meanwhile, Mr. Lakrook said there will be an agitation in the region and accused the Centre of taking the civil society groups, holding talks with it, “for granted”.

“In a few days, an agitation will be launched. We will show how much support we have. In the past, villages were cut off in the name of official functions and were later portrayed as poor participation in our programmes. This time, the agitation will sustain. We will have to struggle and be ready for sacrifices. I ask all to shun any sense of fear,” said Mr. Lakrook.

The Centre-Ladakh talks hit a wall in October this year after the Centre decided against the proposed meeting with the Ladakh civil society group in Delhi on October 22, days after a draft proposal on roadmap by the Centre was criticised by these groups.

In Kargil, the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), a conglomerate of socio-political groups, called for a “complete shutdown” across Kargil on November 10 in protest against the deferment of hill council elections.

“I urge the Lieutenant Governor and the State Election Commissioner (SEC) to consider Ladakh’s geographical and climatic conditions before scheduling polls. Elections in winter could deprive many people of their right to vote. I have also submitted written objections regarding the delimitation exercise,” said Ladakh Member of Parliament (MP) Haji Haneefa.

articles.title: Bengaluru family murders: All seven bodies recovered
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The latest breakthrough came on Monday (November 9, 2026), with the police recovering two more bodies from Shiradi Ghat, in the Western Ghats of Karnataka.

In a significant development in the case of the murders of seven members of a family, which has sent shockwaves across Karnataka, the police have now successfully recovered all seven bodies. The recovery of the bodies was a crucial step in the probe into the ghastly murders, to build a strong case.

The latest breakthrough came on Monday (November 9, 2026), with the police recovering two more bodies from Shiradi Ghat, in the Western Ghats of Karnataka. The bodies have been identified as those of Shankar, the accused Indushekhar’s brother-in-law and his wife, Nalini, who were among the seven victims.

The development comes a day after the police recovered two bodies of the accused’s brother-in-law, Shivakumar and his wife, Divya, from the foothills of Chamundi Hills on Sunday (November 8, 2026). A day before that, the police had recovered two more bodies of the accused’s wife, Sunita and her mother, Roopavathi, from Salem, Tamil Nadu. On November 6, they had recovered the body of a minor boy, Puneeth, 7, from the foothills of Nandi Hills.

The families have decided to conduct the last rites for all seven together in one place. The bodies, most of them found in a highly decomposed state, will be handed over to the family after autopsies have been conducted.

Following a missing complaint by the deceased Nalini’s mother, Tungamma, the Srirampura police on November 5 detained Indushekhar and his 17-year-old minor daughter and rescued an 11-year-old boy from them. The duo confessed to having killed seven members of their family. Indushekhar’s wife, mother-in-law, two brothers-in-law, and their families. The accused has reportedly claimed that marital discord and humiliation by his wife’s family spurred him to take revenge.
A video grab of the Bengaluru police recovering bodies of a family allegedly murdered by a cab driver over domestic disputes. | Photo Credit: Special Arrangement

Meanwhile, police teams investigating the ghastly murders are tracking down shops from which the accused allegedly purchased materials used to dispose of the bodies. Investigators are checking CCTV footage from these shops and recording statements from shop owners and staff to establish the purchases made by the accused and reconstruct his movements before and after the murders.

Police personnel escort accused cab driver Indushekhar in Mysuru, on November 8, 2026. Indushekhar allegedly murdered seven members of his wife’s family, including a seven-year-old boy, over domestic disputes in Bengaluru | Photo Credit: PTI
